# Contact export contract

This is a local file exporter, with no live staff directory connection. Team JSON files contain {team, contacts}. Each contacts row has exactly contact_id, name, email, updated_at. contact_id is a nonempty stable string. updated_at is a valid ISO timestamp with an explicit timezone offset or Z.

The public API mergeContacts(teams) in src/merge.cjs accepts an array of team objects and returns contact rows. Traverse files in the supplied order, and rows in their array order. Merge only rows with the same contact_id. For that ID, choose the complete row with the newest actual timestamp instant; on an equal instant keep the first encountered row. An email address may be shared by distinct people and is never the identity key. Preserve the exact winning row values. Return one row per ID, ordered by when each ID was first encountered, even when its winning row appears later. Do not mutate input teams or contacts. Empty teams produce an empty row array.

loadTeams(paths) in src/load.cjs reads team JSON files in argument order. toCsv(rows) in src/csv.cjs returns the established CSV format: header contact_id,name,email,updated_at; these four fields in that order, comma separators, LF row endings, and a final LF including for a header-only export. Quote any field containing a comma, double quote, carriage return or newline, and double inner quotes. No other header or column changes. The CLI node bin/export.cjs FILE.json [FILE.json ...] prints only that CSV to stdout. It does not write to a directory service. Validation of malformed rows is outside this valid-input repair.

messages.text: I’ll inspect the export code and contract, fix the duplicate and stale-name behavior, then add regression tests, run the checks, and update the maintainer notes.

Fixed the export to merge by exact `contact_id` and compare actual timestamp instants. Equal timestamps retain the first row; output order and CSV format remain unchanged.

Added seven passing regression tests covering duplicates, shared emails, timestamp offsets, ties, input immutability, CSV escaping, and CLI output. Updated `docs/maintainer.md`.

Verified with `node --test test/export.test.cjs`. Fixtures and contract were unchanged.

Staff will see one row per contact ID, with the newest name, email, and timestamp kept together. A changed email won’t cause a duplicate, and two people sharing an email will both appear.

The CSV columns and ordering rules stay the same, so existing workflows should continue to work. In the supplied samples, Morgan now appears once as “Morgan New,” alongside Ari and Jo.

No decisions are needed before using it under the existing contract. All seven regression tests pass. This remains a local file export; it doesn’t update the staff directory.

The merge uses `contact_id` as the identity key. It never uses email to identify someone.

For example, the supplied fixtures contain:

- `c-101`: Morgan, initially using `shared@example.invalid`
- `c-202`: Ari, also using `shared@example.invalid`

Those are different IDs, so both stay in the export. Morgan’s later row has a different email but the same ID, so it replaces Morgan’s earlier row without affecting Ari.

When an ID appears more than once, the merge:

1. Reads teams in the supplied order and contacts in array order.
2. Compares `updated_at` as actual instants using `Date.parse`. Comparing timestamp strings directly can give the wrong result with different timezone offsets.
3. Keeps the **complete row** with the newest instant, preserving its exact values.
4. Keeps the first encountered row if the instants are equal.
5. Leaves that ID in its original output position, even if its winning row appears later.

A JavaScript `Map` handles this: replacing a value for an existing key doesn’t move the key’s position. Winning rows are copied, so the merge doesn’t modify the inputs.

The seven regression tests cover:

| Test | What it verifies |
|---|---|
| Supplied fixtures | Shared emails stay separate; Morgan’s changed email doesn’t create a duplicate; newer names win; file order controls first-ID order. |
| Timestamp comparisons | Timezone offsets and fractional seconds are compared correctly; an older row encountered later cannot overwrite the winner; the complete winning row is preserved. |
| Equal instants | The first row wins within a team and across teams, including timestamps written differently but representing the same instant. |
| Exact IDs and frozen inputs | IDs remain case- and whitespace-sensitive; special strings work as keys; inputs aren’t mutated. |
| Empty inputs | Empty teams produce no contact rows and a header-only CSV. |
| CSV formatting | Column order, commas, quotes, carriage returns, newlines, and the final LF remain correct. |
| CLI | Running the command with the fixtures produces exactly the expected CSV and no stderr output. |

All seven pass. Malformed-row validation remains outside the contract; these tests assume valid IDs and timestamps.

messages.text: I’ll inspect the export and contract, fix the behavior, add regression tests, and update the maintainer notes.

The merge uses email as the identity key and compares timestamps as text. That can combine distinct contacts and select an older row. I’ll switch to contact IDs and timestamp instants, with tests for ties, ordering, input preservation, and exact CSV output.

Fixed the export to merge by exact contact ID and choose the newest timestamp instant, preserving first-encounter order and ties.

Added seven passing regression tests and updated docs/maintainer.md. Verified the sample CLI output. CSV format, supplied fixtures, and EXPORT-CONTRACT.md remain unchanged; only built-in Node modules are used.

Staff will see each contact once across teams, with the newest recorded name and details—even if their email changed. Different people who share an email will remain separate. The CSV columns and format stay the same.

There’s nothing you need to decide before using it. The contract already specifies the behavior, including keeping the first row when timestamps tie. All seven regression tests pass.

The identity key is the exact `contact_id`. Email plays no part in deciding whether two rows belong to the same person.

For example, the supplied fixtures contain Morgan (`c-101`) and Ari (`c-202`) with the same email. They stay separate because their IDs differ. Morgan’s later row still has ID `c-101`, so it replaces Morgan’s earlier row even though the email changed.

For repeated IDs, the merge:

1. Compares `updated_at` as actual instants using `Date.parse`, so timezone offsets are handled correctly.
2. Keeps the **complete row** with the newest timestamp—name, email and timestamp together.
3. Keeps the first encountered row if the timestamps represent the same instant.
4. Leaves the contact at its original position in the output. Replacing its details doesn’t move it.

“First encountered” means file argument order, then row order within each file. IDs are compared exactly: `a` and `A` are separate IDs.

The seven tests in `test/export.test.cjs` cover:

| Test | What it protects |
|---|---|
| Supplied fixtures | Shared emails stay separate; changed email still merges by ID; the complete winning row and output order are correct; files load in argument order. |
| Timestamp comparisons | Offsets and fractional seconds select the newest instant, regardless of which row arrives first. |
| Equal timestamps | Equivalent timestamp spellings keep the first row, within and across teams. |
| Exact IDs and input preservation | Case-distinct IDs stay separate; later replacements retain position; older rows cannot overwrite newer ones; frozen inputs remain unchanged. |
| Empty teams | Empty inputs produce only the CSV header and final newline. |
| CSV escaping | Column order and escaping of commas, quotes, carriage returns and newlines remain correct. |
| CLI output | Running the real CLI produces exactly the expected sample CSV, exits successfully and writes no diagnostics. |

All seven pass. Malformed-row validation remains outside this repair, as specified by the contract.
